Each task changes a production system that must keep running.

In the system design tasks the agent makes a multi-process service hold its guarantees through crashes, retries, races and returning stale writers, and hidden tests kill or pause processes to check them.
In the infrastructure tasks the agent restructures live Terraform or Pulumi code so that the plan against production state changes nothing that is deployed.
Gemini 4 Argon passes 20% of its runs on these tasks, and it fails every run on 44% of the tasks.
Gemini 3.8 Flash passes 10%, and it fails every run on 73% of the tasks.
The main languages are HCL (Terraform) (33%), Go (31%) and Python (13%).

| Domain | What the tasks do | % of catalog |
|---|---|---:|
| State-preserving infrastructure changes | Split flat Terraform stacks into modules, or port them to Pulumi, without replacing any deploye
Engineers here change production systems that must keep running.

In services where several processes share state and any of them can stop, the failures are duplicate effects after retries, lost notifications, stale writers returning after a takeover, limits that hold in one process but not across instances, and partial state after a crash.
In infrastructure code, a flat Terraform stack has to become modules with stable keys, or move to Pulumi, while every deployed resource stays exactly as it is.
Service tasks pin an open-source repository at a base commit and give a short specification, often with time limits.
The agent runs the databases, caches or brokers it needs locally and delivers a patch.
Hidden tests then kill or pause processes and confirm that existing behaviour still works.
Infrastructure tasks ship the stack with its recorded production state and an offline toolchain.
A separate verifier plans the result with refresh disabled and expects moves only, then plans hidden changes such as an added key.
A capability gap stated as "X cannot do Y", followed by measurable requirements, many with time limits.
A closing paragraph with the repository path, how to start each service and the build command.
A first-person request to modularize a named production Terraform stack, followed by rules for modules, `for_each` keys, variables, outputs and banned constructs.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A backend engineer on a self-hosted budgeting app needs the sync server to compact each budget's change log from a client-built snapshot without breaking offline devices.
The engineer starts from the sync server, CRDT and client packages, and the server cannot read the encrypted changes it stores.

The hard part is the protocol: a conditional checkpoint commit tied to a receive base, correct handling of late messages with older timestamps, and compatibility for old clients, all checked across several simulated devices.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A maintainer of a container registry replaces long-lived, project-wide scanner robot accounts with short-lived credentials scoped to one repository.
The engineer starts from Harbor's core and jobservice code for scan jobs, robot accounts and registry authorization.

The hard part is the lifecycle across processes: keeping secrets out of Redis job records and logs, keeping the credential valid during long scans, and revoking it when a job ends or when jobservice dies without a final hook.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A backend engineer running a NuGet server as several replicas over shared PostgreSQL and S3 must make package-version writes safe under races, partitions and crashes.
The engineer starts from BaGetter's push, delete, mirror and storage code.

The hard part is fencing: a writer whose database claim has expired must not overwrite or delete the winner's objects, and a new reconcile endpoint must clean up orphans while old-layout packages and an existing schema keep working.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A platform engineer inherits a production alert-routing stack written as one flat root module with list-indexed resources and hard-coded settings.
The engineer must split it into eventing, messaging and processing modules keyed by team, source, severity and channel, with generalized variables and outputs.
The hard part is expressing every address change in configuration so the plan against the live state contains only moves, while passing IDs between modules through outputs instead of literals.
